metric_rationale: The experimental design pits Take The Best against Tallying such that they predict exactly opposite choices on every single trial. This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the Take The Best prediction (which relies solely on the highest-validity discriminating cue). For data simulated under Take The Best, this value will be close to 1. For data simulated under Tallying, which favors the numerical majority of cues (always the opposite option in this design), this value will be close to 0.

The experiment is explicitly designed such that the Tallying heuristic and the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic make opposite predictions on all 8 trial types. This metric computes the proportion of choices that match the strict Tallying prediction (i.e., choosing the option with the greater number of winning features). Under the Tallying theory, this proportion will be significantly greater than 0.5 (approaching 1 depending on noise parameters), whereas under TTB it will be significantly less than 0.5 (approaching 0).

The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against Weighted Additive (WADD) models such that they make diametrically opposed predictions on every trial. TTB invariably chooses the option favored by the single highest-validity discriminating cue, whereas WADD favors the alternative option backed by a coalition of lower-validity cues. By computing the proportion of trials where the subject's choice aligns with the TTB prediction, we will obtain values close to 1 for TTB-simulated data and values close to 0 for WADD-simulated data, providing a maximal, highly reliable contrast between the two theories.

The experimental design pits Take The Best (TTB) against the Weighted Additive (WADD) strategy by pairing a single highly valid cue favoring one option against multiple slightly less valid cues favoring the other. Because the validities are closely spaced, WADD (even with extreme non-linear transformations) will consistently favor the option supported by the coalition of cues, whereas TTB will invariably choose the option supported by the single best cue. This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the TTB prediction. Under TTB, this value will be close to 1 (minus noise); under WADD, it will be close to 0 (plus noise). This diametrical opposition guarantees maximal discrimination between the two theories.

If the Position Bias (Task Disengagement) theory is correct, the probability of choosing Option A vs B is determined solely by a spatial/positional bias and is completely independent of the feature ratings. Consequently, the empirical proportion of choosing Option B should be roughly the same across all 8 unique trial types, resulting in a very low variance across trial types (driven only by binomial sampling noise, max ~0.02). Conversely, the Weighted Additive (WADD) theory predicts that choice probabilities strongly depend on the feature values, meaning some trial types will heavily favor Option A and others Option B. This will result in a much higher variance of choice proportions across the 8 trial types (up to ~0.25).

This metric computes the difference in the probability of choosing Option A when Option A is objectively superior (higher weighted sum of features) versus when Option B is objectively superior. Under the WADD strategy, subjects are sensitive to feature values, so they will choose A much more often when it is superior, resulting in a large positive difference. Under Position Bias, subjects ignore the features and choose A with a constant probability across all trials, resulting in a difference near zero.
